questions.question: Which of the following are part of the Model Context Protocol's official project scope? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The MCP Specification
Language-specific MCP SDKs
Development tools such as the MCP Inspector
A hosted LLM inference service
Reference server implementations

questions.explanation: MCP's scope covers the specification, SDKs, development tools (like the Inspector), and reference server implementations. MCP does not provide model inference and doesn't dictate how applications use LLMs.

questions.question: According to the intro docs, which stakeholders gain the listed benefit from MCP? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Developers: reduced development time and complexity when building or integrating with AI applications
AI applications/agents: access to an ecosystem of data sources, tools, and apps
End users: more capable AI applications that can access their data and act on their behalf
GPU vendors: reduced memory bandwidth requirements

questions.explanation: The intro lists exactly these three beneficiary groups. Hardware efficiency is not part of MCP's value proposition.

questions.question: Which of the following are examples the documentation gives of what MCP can enable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Agents accessing Google Calendar and Notion as a personalized assistant
Claude Code generating a web app from a Figma design
Enterprise chatbots connecting to multiple databases for chat-based analysis
AI models creating 3D designs in Blender and printing them on a 3D printer
Training a foundation model on private data

questions.explanation: All four are flagship examples in the intro. Model training is out of scope — MCP is about context exchange, not model development.

questions.question: Which statements about MCP's design philosophy are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: MCP focuses solely on the protocol for context exchange
MCP dictates how AI applications must manage the context they receive
MCP takes inspiration from the Language Server Protocol
It reduces the M×N integration problem to roughly M+N implementations
MCP requires all servers to be open source

questions.explanation: MCP deliberately does NOT dictate LLM usage or context management, and both open- and closed-source servers exist (the registry supports both). The LSP parallel and the M×N→M+N reduction are core framing.

questions.question: Per the specification overview, MCP provides a standardized way for applications to... (Select all that apply.)

options.text: share contextual information with language models
expose tools and capabilities to AI systems
build composable integrations and workflows
train and fine-tune foundation models
All of the above

questions.explanation: The spec names exactly three: sharing context, exposing tools/capabilities, and composable integrations. Model training is out of scope, which also makes 'All of the above' wrong.

questions.question: Which are core server primitives defined by the MCP specification? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Tools — callable functions invoked by the model
Resources — readable context identified by URI
Prompts — reusable templates the user selects
Sessions — durable server-side conversation state
All of the above

questions.explanation: Tools, resources, and prompts are the three server primitives. Protocol-level sessions were removed in 2026-07-28 (SEP-2567), so D — and therefore 'All of the above' — is wrong.

questions.question: Which statements about MCP's governance artifacts are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Specification changes are proposed via SEPs with PR-derived numbering
Official extensions live in ext-prefixed repositories under the modelcontextprotocol GitHub org
The specification uses BCP 14 / RFC 2119 keywords (MUST, SHOULD, MAY)
SEPs are approved by a public token-holder vote
All of the above

questions.explanation: SEPs go through sponsors and maintainer review via PR labels — there is no token vote. A–C are accurate, so the all-of-the-above trap fails on D.

questions.question: MCP reduces integration effort because... (Select all that apply.)

options.text: each AI application implements the client side of the protocol once
each external system exposes one MCP server usable by any compliant client
M applications × N systems collapses from M×N custom connectors to roughly M+N implementations
every server must be rewritten for each new host application
All of the above

questions.explanation: D describes the world MCP replaces. The M+N economics only work because servers are host-agnostic.
